title: Advanced Pitfalls in A/B Experimentation
description: Master common experiment pitfalls including peeking, multiple comparisons, Simpson's paradox, and interaction effects.

interactions.prompt: What is the most likely consequence of checking your A/B test results daily and stopping when p < 0.05?

options.text: Inflated false positive rate far above 5%
Deflated false positive rate below 5%
No effect on error rates whatsoever
Only affects false negative rate

interactions.teachingPreamble: The 'peeking problem' is one of the most common A/B testing pitfalls. When Airbnb's experimentation team analyzed their tests, they found that repeatedly checking results and stopping early inflated false positive rates to 20-30%, far above the intended 5%. Sequential testing frameworks like those used by Netflix solve this by adjusting significance boundaries over time.

interactions.prompt: A Spotify team runs 20 independent A/B tests on a new playlist algorithm, all at α = 0.05. One test shows p = 0.03. No corrections are applied. What's the key concern?

options.text: Sample size was likely too small
Expected ~1 false positive among 20 tests by chance alone
The p-value is too close to 0.05 threshold
Playlist algorithms can't be A/B tested

chartData.title: Expected vs Observed Significant Results (20 Tests, α = 0.05)

interactions.prompt: Which correction method controls the false discovery rate while preserving more statistical power than Bonferroni?

options.text: Bonferroni correction
Benjamini-Hochberg procedure
Simply increasing sample size
Running tests sequentially instead of simultaneously

interactions.teachingPreamble: When running multiple comparisons, Bonferroni correction (dividing α by the number of tests) is the simplest fix but is overly conservative—it dramatically reduces your power to detect real effects. At LinkedIn, data scientists frequently use the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, which controls the false discovery rate (the expected proportion of false positives among rejected hypotheses) rather than the family-wise error rate, giving substantially more power.

interactions.prompt: Simpson's paradox occurs when a trend that appears in subgroups ____ when the groups are combined, often due to a lurking confounding variable.

options.text: Reverses or disappears
Becomes statistically significant
Doubles in magnitude
Stays exactly the same

interactions.prompt: Your DoorDash team's A/B test shows a new checkout flow increases conversion by 4% overall (p=0.01), but segmented analysis reveals it hurts conversion by 6% for mobile users (60% of traffic). Ship the change or hold?

options.text: Ship it—the overall result is significant and positive
Hold and investigate the mobile segment before any decision
Ship only for desktop users immediately
Rerun the entire test with a larger sample

interactions.prompt: A Booking.com test shows +3% revenue per user but -1.5% in bookings per user. What advanced pitfall does this illustrate?

options.text: Peeking problem from early stopping
Metric conflict requiring an Overall Evaluation Criterion
Novelty effect that will fade over time
Selection bias from non-random assignment

interactions.teachingPreamble: Experienced experimentation teams track guardrail metrics alongside their primary metric to catch unintended harm. Booking.com, which runs thousands of tests annually, uses an Overall Evaluation Criterion (OEC)—a composite metric that balances short-term revenue against long-term user engagement. Without an OEC, teams often optimize one metric while silently degrading another, creating an illusion of improvement.

interactions.prompt: Rank these experiment threats from most to least likely to cause a false positive in a typical product A/B test: (a) Novelty effect, (b) Peeking and early stopping, (c) Unequal sample ratio due to a bug, (d) Day-of-week seasonality in a 3-day test.

options.text: Novelty effect inflating early engagement
Peeking at results and stopping early
Sample ratio mismatch from an engineering bug
Day-of-week seasonality in a short test

interactions.prompt: Your team already corrected for multiple comparisons using Benjamini-Hochberg. Now you discover that 40% of users in the treatment group were also exposed to a simultaneous pricing experiment. What should you do?

options.text: Results are fine—Benjamini-Hochberg already handles interaction effects
Analyze only users not exposed to the pricing test
Discard the test entirely and start over
Double the Benjamini-Hochberg correction factor

interactions.priorContext: Previously you corrected for multiple comparisons assuming independent tests. Now a cross-experiment contamination has been discovered—40% of treatment users were simultaneously in another experiment that changed pricing, violating the independence assumption and potentially confounding your results.
